To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the growth of FCC crystals on (100) templates is defect-free, (ii) growth on other templates results in amorphous sedimentation if the dimensionless particle flux exceeds a critical value that is orientation dependent, and (iii) extended defects can nucleation and grow if the crystal exceeds the critical thickness that depends only on the lattice misfits.

(1) rapid, controlled growth of defect-free colloidal crystal films is achieved only onto (100) substrates and (2) this growth is controlled by a competition between the flux of colloidal particles and the rate of defect nucleation.

the rapid growth of colloidal crystals is possible on FCC (100) substrates and that the growth of colloidal single crystals is possible on any crystallographic orientation if the lattice misfit is sufficiently small.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the crystal growth is controlled by the crystal structure and not by the crystal orientation.
the (100) orientation is the only orientation for which the crystal can grow without any defects.
the growth of colloidal crystals is a complex process that depends strongly on the crystal structure, lattice mismatch, and deposition conditions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that the growth of colloidal crystals is a very complex process and that there are a number of parameters that can be used to tune the quality of colloidal crystals.
the growth of large, high-quality colloidal crystals is possible if the crystal orientation, growth conditions, and template orientation are carefully matched.
the (100) template is the best choice for the growth of defect-free, monodisperse FCC colloidal crystals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the growth conditions can be chosen to avoid the formation of extended defects in the crystal, and thus to produce defect-free colloidal single crystals.
the growth of colloidal crystals can be controlled by selecting the template orientation.
growth onto (100)-oriented templates is a robust, scalable, and inexpensive way to produce large, defect-free FCC colloidal crystals.
